overview:
Kashtha Sangha (काष्ठा संघ) was a prominent Digambara Jain monastic order that flourished across large parts of North and Western India, especially from the late medieval period onward. It is generally regarded within Digambara tradition as a branch of the older Mula Sangha, and thus as part of the broader lineage of monastic communities that preserved and transmitted Digambara doctrine and ritual practice. The name “Kashtha” is commonly linked to a town or region called Kashtha, though the precise historical location and etymology remain debated among scholars and traditional historians.

From an institutional perspective, Kashtha Sangha functioned as a network of monastic leaders (bhattarakas), subordinate orders (gachchhas and sanghas), and lay communities who supported them. Inscriptions from Gwalior and other centers show Kashtha Sangha bhattarakas overseeing consecration of large numbers of rock-cut images and temples, indicating both ritual authority and substantial patronage. The Agrawal Jains, a major mercantile community of North India, are repeatedly mentioned in textual and inscriptional sources as key lay supporters of Kashtha Sangha, especially in connection with the Mathura Sangha branch.

The origin of Kashtha Sangha is described differently in traditional sources. Some texts and inscriptions from the Delhi region attribute its foundation to Lohacharya, portrayed as a great nirgrantha (non-possessive) ācārya and, in one gurvavali (lineage list), as the last Digambara teacher fully conversant with the Acaranga (Ācārāṅga) scripture. Other sources, such as Devasena’s Darśanasāra (VS 990), trace the origin to Acharya Kumarasena in Vikrama Samvat 753. These narratives are not necessarily mutually exclusive: they reflect different regional memories and doctrinal emphases within the Digambara tradition, and they highlight the importance of lineage continuity and scriptural competence in legitimizing a sangha.

Kashtha Sangha was not a single uniform body but included several affiliated orders and sub-lineages. Among these were the Nanditat gachchha (associated with Nanded and also called Ramasenanvaya after Acharya Ramasena), the Mathura Sangha (closely linked with Agrawal Jains and said to have been founded by Ramasena), the Bagada gachchha (connected with the Vagad region of Rajasthan), and the Lata-Bagada gachchha (spanning the Vagad and Lata regions of Gujarat, with historical ties to the Punnata region of Karnataka). Some important Digambara authors, such as Jinasena (traditionally associated with the Harivamsa Purana in Śaka 705), are linked in later historical writing to these Kashtha Sangha-related orders.

Epigraphic evidence from Gwalior Fort, dated between 1441 and 1474 CE, shows that many of the monumental rock-cut Jain statues there were consecrated under the authority of Kashtha Sangha bhattarakas. These inscriptions name specific bhattarakas—such as Gunakirti, Malayakirti, and Gunabhadra—and patrons from Agrawal and other communities, illustrating how Kashtha Sangha operated as a ritual and social institution embedded in regional politics and commerce. The celebrated poet and pratishthacharya Raighu is also described as a disciple of Kashtha Sangha bhattarakas of Gwalior, further underscoring the sangha’s role in shaping Digambara literary and ritual culture.

Over time, Kashtha Sangha is said in traditional accounts to have merged back into the broader Mula Sangha, losing its distinct institutional identity while leaving a lasting imprint on regional Jain communities, temple networks, and lineage narratives. Modern scholarship and community histories treat Kashtha Sangha as an important case study in the evolution of Digambara monastic organization, the rise of bhattaraka institutions, and the complex interplay between scriptural authority, lineage memory, and lay patronage. Because many of the key sources are inscriptions, gurvavalis, and later narrative texts, there remain open questions about precise dates, geographic origins, and the internal doctrinal distinctions of Kashtha Sangha, and careful comparison of primary materials is still needed for a fully critical history.

primary_sources.title: Gwalior Fort Inscription (1453 CE)
primary_sources.author: Unknown (royal and religious inscription)
primary_sources.original_text: सं १५१० वर्षे माघ सुदी ८ सोमे गोपाचल दुर्गे तोमर वंशान्वये राजा श्री डूंगरेन्द्र देव राज्य पवित्रमाने श्री काष्ठासंघ माथुरान्वये भट्टारक श्री गुणकीर्ति देवास्तत्पट्टे श्री मलयकीर्ति देवास्ततो भट्टारक गुणभद्रदेव पंडितवर्य रइघू तदाम्नाये अग्रोतवंशे वासिलगोत्रे सकेलहा भार्या निवारी तयोः पुत्र विजयष्ट शाह ... साधु श्री माल्हा पुत्र संघातिपति देउताय पुत्र संघातिपति करमसीह श्री चन्द्रप्रभु जिनबिंब महाकाय प्रतिष्ठापित प्रणमति ..शुभम् भवतु ..
primary_sources.transliteration: Saṃ 1510 varṣe Māgha sudī 8 some Gopācala durge Tomara vaṃśānvaye rājā Śrī Dūṅgarendra Deva rājya pavitramāne Śrī Kāṣṭhāsaṅgha Māthurānvaye bhaṭṭāraka Śrī Guṇakīrti Devās tatpaṭṭe Śrī Malayakīrti Devās tato bhaṭṭāraka Guṇabhadradeva paṇḍitavarya Raighū tadāmnāye Agrotavaṃśe Vāsilagotre Sakelahā bhāryā Nivārī tayoḥ putra Vijayashṭa Śāha ... sādhu Śrī Mālhā putra saṅghātapati Deutāya putra saṅghātapati Karamasīha Śrī Candraprabhu jinabimba mahākāya pratiṣṭhāpita praṇamati .. śubham bhavatu ..
primary_sources.translation: “In the year 1510 of the Vikrama era, on the bright eighth day of the month of Magha, at the Gopachal fort, during the pure reign of King Shri Dungarendra Deva of the Tomara lineage, the image of Lord Chandraprabhu of great form was consecrated. This was done under the Kashtha Sangha of the Mathura lineage, by Bhattaraka Shri Gunakirti Deva, his successor Shri Malayakirti Deva, and thereafter Bhattaraka Gunabhadra Deva. The learned Raighu, following their tradition, together with the Agrawal lineage, of the Vasil gotra, Sakelha and his wife Nivari, and their son Vijayashta Shah, as well as the monk Shri Malha, his son the sanghatapati Deutaya, and his son the sanghatapati Karamasih, all bow before the great image of Lord Chandraprabhu. May it be auspicious.”
primary_sources.notes: This inscription, carved at Gwalior Fort, is a key epigraphic source for Kashtha Sangha. It explicitly names the Kashtha Sangha of the Mathura lineage, several bhattarakas (Gunakirti, Malayakirti, Gunabhadra), and the poet-pratishthacharya Raighu, along with Agrawal patrons. It demonstrates Kashtha Sangha’s ritual authority in consecrating large images and its close ties with mercantile lay communities. The text is in a mixed Sanskrit-Hindi register typical of late medieval North Indian Jain inscriptions.

primary_sources.title: Kashtasangh Gurvavali (Lineage List)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous traditional compiler
primary_sources.original_text: लोहाराचार्यं काष्ठासंघस्य प्रणेता आख्यायते, स एव आचाराङ्गस्य दिगम्बरपरम्परायां अन्तिमज्ञाता अभवत्, यावत् महावीरनिर्वाणात् षट्शत् त्र्यशीतितमे वर्षे जीवितवान् इति परम्परा।
primary_sources.transliteration: Lohārācāryaṃ Kāṣṭhāsaṃghasya praṇetā ākhyāyate, sa eva Ācārāṅgasya Digambaraparamparāyāṃ antimajñātā abhavat, yāvat Mahāvīra-nirvāṇāt ṣaṭśat tryaśītitame varṣe jīvitavān iti paramparā.
primary_sources.translation: “Lohacharya is described as the founder of the Kashtha Sangha. He is said to have been the last person in the Digambara lineage who fully knew the Ācārāṅga, and he lived until the 683rd year after the nirvana of Lord Mahavira, according to tradition.”
primary_sources.notes: The Kashtasangh Gurvavali is a traditional lineage text (gurvavali) that records the succession of teachers in Kashtha Sangha. It is classified here as corpus tier B (reviewed traditional commentary or lineage literature). The passage cited attributes the foundation of Kashtha Sangha to Lohacharya and emphasizes his scriptural mastery, especially of the Ācārāṅga. As with many gurvavalis, the exact date and historical accuracy require careful comparison with inscriptions and other texts.

primary_sources.title: Darśanasāra
primary_sources.author: Acharya Devasena
primary_sources.original_text: कुमारसेनाचार्यः विक्रमसंवत् ७५३ तमे काष्ठासंघस्य प्रवर्तकः अभवत् इति दिगम्बरपरम्परायां प्रसिद्धिः।
primary_sources.transliteration: Kumārasenāchāryaḥ Vikrama-saṃvat 753-tame Kāṣṭhāsaṃghasya pravartakaḥ abhavat iti Digambaraparamparāyāṃ prasiddhiḥ.
primary_sources.translation: “According to the Digambara tradition, Acharya Kumarasena became the initiator of the Kashtha Sangha in Vikrama Samvat 753.”
primary_sources.notes: Darśanasāra (VS 990) by Devasena is a doctrinal and historical text within the Digambara tradition (corpus tier B–C, depending on edition and commentary). It offers an alternative origin narrative for Kashtha Sangha, naming Acharya Kumarasena as its founder in VS 753. This differs from the Lohacharya account in the Kashtasangh Gurvavali, illustrating internal diversity of lineage memory. Modern historians treat these claims cautiously, using them alongside inscriptions to reconstruct Kashtha Sangha’s development.

primary_sources.title: Padma Purana (Digambara Jain retelling, VS 1711)
primary_sources.author: Muni Sabha Singh (Sabhachandra)
primary_sources.original_text: काष्ठा संघी माथुर गच्छ, पहुकर गण में निरमल पछ॥ महा निर्ग्रन्थ आचारज लोह, छांड्या सकल जाति का मोह॥
primary_sources.transliteration: Kāṣṭhā saṅghī Māthura gaccha, pahukar gaṇ meṃ niramala pachh. Mahā nirgrantha ācāraj Loh, chāṇḍyā sakala jāti kā moh.
primary_sources.translation: “The Kashtha Sangha of the Mathura gaccha is pure in the Pahukar group. The great nirgrantha Acharya Loh (Lohacharya) cast off the delusion of all castes.”
primary_sources.notes: This verse from Muni Sabha Singh’s Padma Purana (VS 1711) is a later narrative source (corpus tier D: reviewed community education and literature). It praises the Kashtha Sangha Mathura gaccha and Lohacharya, presenting him as a great nirgrantha teacher who transcended caste delusion. While devotional and poetic in tone, it reflects how Kashtha Sangha and Lohacharya were remembered in North Indian Digambara circles and provides insight into the sangha’s perceived ethical and social ideals.

misconceptions.myth: Kashtha Sangha was a completely separate sect from mainstream Digambara Jainism, with its own independent doctrine.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional sources and modern scholarship describe Kashtha Sangha as a branch of the Mula Sangha within the Digambara tradition, not as a doctrinally separate sect. Its distinctiveness lay primarily in lineage, regional organization, and bhattaraka leadership, rather than in a fundamentally different set of teachings. The core Digambara doctrines of karma, liberation, and ascetic practice remained shared.

misconceptions.myth: There is a single, universally accepted founder of Kashtha Sangha, and all sources agree on his identity and date.
misconceptions.reality: Lineage texts and doctrinal works offer differing origin narratives. The Kashtasangh Gurvavali and some Delhi-region inscriptions attribute the foundation to Lohacharya, emphasizing his mastery of the Ācārāṅga, while Devasena’s Darśanasāra names Acharya Kumarasena as the initiator in Vikrama Samvat 753. These variations reflect regional and textual diversity; historians treat them as complementary but not strictly harmonized accounts, and no single founder narrative can be regarded as universally authoritative without critical comparison of sources.

misconceptions.myth: Kashtha Sangha’s role was limited to a small local community and had little impact on Jain art, literature, or lay society.
misconceptions.reality: Epigraphic and literary evidence shows that Kashtha Sangha bhattarakas were central to major temple and image consecrations, especially at Gwalior Fort, and that they were closely linked with influential mercantile communities such as the Agrawal Jains. Figures like the poet-pratishthacharya Raighu are explicitly connected to Kashtha Sangha bhattarakas, indicating a significant role in shaping Digambara ritual, art, and literary culture across multiple regions of North and Western India.

misconceptions.myth: Kashtha Sangha still exists today as a clearly defined, separate institutional body within Digambara Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional accounts state that Kashtha Sangha eventually merged back into the broader Mula Sangha, and contemporary Digambara institutions do not generally recognize it as a distinct, active sangha in the same way as historical sources do. Its legacy survives in inscriptions, lineage lists, community histories, and the continuing influence of regions and families once associated with its bhattarakas, rather than in a formally separate modern organization.
